subtopics: "Parties involved" — Apex Bank (a Tennessee retail bank without credit cards) versus CC Serve Corp. (credit‑card service provider).
"Apex’s proposed marks" — an ‘ASPIRE BANK’ word mark together with an accompanying design mark intended for internet‐banking services.
"CC Serve’s existing priority" — registration No. 2126948 for the word mark ‘ASPIRE’ issued in 1998 with priority date October 17 1996.
"Chronology" — intent‑to‑use filings (Aug 2019), publication (Dec 17 2019), opposition filed by CC Serve (Feb 2020), refusal order under §2(d) issued by the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board.
"Jurisdictional elements" — appeal brought under §1295(a)(4)(B); Federal Circuit’s de‑novo review standards cited.
"Lanham Act provision" — Section 2(d) allows a prior user to contest registration until priority date.
"Likelihood‑of‑confusion test" — central analytical engine consisting of thirteen DuPont factors.
"Standard of review" — appellate courts decide facts de‑novo against substantial evidence while applying DuPont questions as matters of law.
"Relevant precedents" — M2 Software v. M2 Communications establishes de‑novo/substantial‐evidence split; DuPont points distinguish similarity among goods/services.
"Second DUONT factor” — services declared highly similar following dictionary bases (‘credit card services’ equals ‘banking’ + ‘finance’); Board affirmed.

"Sixth DUONT factor” — board limited comparison to nine third‑party Aspire designs tied strictly to credit‑card services, deeming them ‘not considerable,’ thereby granting CC Serve normal protection over inherently distinctive marks.
"First DUONT factor” — overall commercial impression judged adverse toward Apex based on similarities noted elsewhere.
"Other DUONT factors” — omitted because the Board felt they were either irrelevant or outweighed by findings already set.
"Affirmation of Second Factor” — court concurred that factual inferential support was compelling enough for similarity determination;

"Vacating Sixth Factor” — court held restricting third‑party mark universe narrowly contradicted Rule that similarity concerns goods/services marked during priority hearing; full commonsense scope warranted.
"Vacating First Factor” — recognition that commercial impression hinges partly upon perceived scope revealed via sixth‑factor scope imbalance warranted reconsideration.
"Judicial outcome" — affirmed finder regarding second DUONT input while vacating determinations concerning sixth and first factors pending remand.
"Scope implications" — secondary interpretation demonstrates strict adherence against arbitrary narrowing measures when service similarity has already been established.
"Future counterexamples” — illustrates exceptional caution when dosing third‑party mark evaluations—a narrower field can unjustifiably shadow effects across unrelated products/services.
